articles.title_zh: EU and China to hold two-day talks in Beijing to avert trade war
articles.content_orig:
Brussels, Belgium – EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic will head to Beijing on Thursday for two days of make-or-break meetings with Chinese officials to try to stave off a trade war.
The European Union has toughened its stance towards Beijing to defend businesses against what it believes is unfair competition in critical sectors including cars.
Increasingly, European leaders and observers warn of a “China Shock 2.0,” used to describe Chinese firms’ shift into more high-tech manufacturing, which is threatening many traditional EU industries.

articles.title_orig: ‘Unwelcome and unsafe’: Why Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate
articles.title_zh: ‘Unwelcome and unsafe’: Why Japanese companies are retreating from China at a historic rate
articles.content_orig:
Japanese companies are leaving China in record numbers, as a slowing Chinese economy and a diplomatic freeze force businesses to reassess their presence in the world's second-largest economy.
The number of Japanese companies operating in China fell to a historic low, standing at 10,118 as of June, according to Teikoku Databank , a corporate credit research firm in Japan. That's down 22% from the previous survey held in June 2024 and about 30% below the 2012 peak, and the lowest since Teikoku began tracking the data in 2010.
Japanese firms, which were already planning to reduce their footprint in China, are considering withdrawing from the market with greater urgency since China-Japan ties went into a tailspin, said Jeremy Chan, an analyst at political consultancy firm Eurasia Group.
The exodus is likely to intensify as the diplomatic feud between Asia's top two economies forces Japanese companies — already grappling with shrinking profitability strained by tariff risks, growing labor and manufacturing costs, cutthroat local competition — to shrink or shut their operation in China, Teikoku said in its report last week. Some firms have reduced dependence on China without fully decoupling from it, it added.
China-Japan relations have come under heavy strain since Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament in November last year that Japan could get militarily involved in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan. Beijing has responded by curbing exports of critical minerals to Japanese companies and urged citizens to refrain from traveling to Japan.
Factors such as U.S. tariffs and a growing public resistance to Chinese goods and a growing Indian market have also further incentivised Japanese businesses' push to diversify away from Beijing, said Martin Schulz, chief policy economist at Fujitsu Research Institute. "Investment in China is weathering the perfect storm," he said.
In the past two years, a record number of 4,137 Japanese companies fully withdrew from China, according to Teikoku's data. Only 1,221 entered over the same period, through subsidiaries, factories or representative offices, the fewest on record outside the Covid-19 pandemic.
Japanese firms have grown increasingly reliant on the U.S. market while shifting away from China, what was once a key market, said Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group.
Topix-listed companies saw the share of profits derived in China dwindle to less than 15% so far this year, down from 23% in 2020, while those from the U.S. rose to 35% compared with 25% over the same period, according to Koll's estimates.
Washington is "openly courting" Japanese players to aid its re-industrialization efforts while Beijing has shifted towards a "made in and made by China" model, Koll said.
Cases of Japanese nationals being detained by Beijing this year have further added to businesses' concerns about sending personnel to China, analysts say. Several Japanese nationals, including executives at top Japanese firms, were reportedly detained in August over alleged violations of dual-use goods export restrictions.
"Japanese firms and their employees increasingly feel unwelcome and unsafe in China," Chan said.
An April report from Japan External Trade Organization showed that companies are increasingly reluctant to expand their business in China.
On Tuesday, a day after the Teikoku report, Chinese vice premier He Lifeng said China "always welcomes" Japanese enterprises to develop business and share market opportunities in the country.
He told a delegation from the Japanese Association for the Promotion of International Trade to "keep to the right course on historical issues … and play a greater role in advancing China-Japan economic and trade cooperation."
Automakers, parts suppliers and export-oriented manufacturers are the most likely to scale back in China, said Kei Koga, a professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. Companies that have localized and can compete with Chinese rivals, particularly medical and precision equipment makers, are more likely to stay, he added.

articles.title_orig: Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years
articles.title_zh: Chinese man, 71, discovers hidden US$63,000 fortune after scavenging for 21 years
articles.content_orig:
Handing Ru the bank card, a social worker advised him to keep it safe, spend wisely, and beware of telecom scams
An elderly man in central China, who has spent the past 21 years making ends meet as a scavenger, experienced a remarkable stroke of luck when he discovered that his pension fund contained over 420,000 yuan (US$63,000).
In late September, the 71-year-old man, surnamed Ru, received a bank card linked to his pension account, which revealed a balance of 424,204 yuan, as reported by Changde Daily.
Completely unaware of his entitlement to pensions over the decades, Ru sobbed as he spoke to the media: “It goes without saying that I am happy. I never expected this to happen. I am grateful for the support from the social assistance authority and other related government departments.”
For the past 21 years, Ru has been scavenging to earn a living in Changde, Hunan province.

articles.title_orig: France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
articles.title_zh: France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
articles.content_orig:
France plans to fully or partially close up to 500 schools on Monday amid a series of student protests that have become increasingly violent .
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced the precautionary measures on Sunday as part of a bid for a “partial, progressive return to lessons”. However, after a weekend lull, student protestors announced they plan to resume demonstrations – launched last month over complaints regarding class sizes, lack of teachers, and other complaints – early in the week.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the minister said. He added that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the protests.
Geffray said the closures were a security precaution. Protest organisers have called for a return to large-scale demonstrations on Tuesday, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
At least 170 students and 78 educational personnel have been injured since the student demos first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September, according to Geffray.
The Ministry of National Education reported that at least 400 of the 3,700 high schools in France were closed on Friday , while 560 faced protests or disruptions.
The number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday, Geffray said.
Teachers and students first mobilised at a high school in a Paris suburb on 17 September over a lack of teaching staff, excessive school-day hours and other grievances . The protests have since spread nationwide, resulting in class strikes, blockades and demonstrations.
According to the interior minister, more than 5,000 people have been arrested in the last week; 85 percent of them minors.
Critics have criticised “disproportionate” police violence in response to the demonstrations. Rights group Amnesty International said the student protestors “must be listened to, not repressed”.
In an interview on French public radio, Geffray claimed far-left activists “infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves and engaged in extreme violence.”

articles.title_orig: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.title_zh: Polish activists launch abortion pill locker to bypass near-total ban
articles.content_orig:
‘AbortOmat’ in Warsaw offers novel way to challenge country’s restrictions and allow women swift, anonymous access
They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind last week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
after newsletter promotion
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

articles.title_orig: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.title_zh: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.content_orig:
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.
Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.
Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.
“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told Al Jazeera.
“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.
It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.
RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.
But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.
On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.
Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.
On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.
“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.
“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”
US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.
“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain – it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”
Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.
The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.
RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.
The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.
Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases, including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia, in March.

articles.title_orig: U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. air base following security incident
articles.title_zh: U.S. military removes bombers from U.K. air base following security incident
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force has removed all of its bombers from a U.K. air base following a security incident that led to the arrest of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national last month, a Pentagon spokesperson confirmed to CBS News on Sunday.
All U.S. bombers deployed to RAF Fairford have been returned to their home stations in the United States, the spokesperson said. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the bombers' return.
"U.S. Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements," the Pentagon spokesperson's statement said. "The Airmen that operate America's bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime."
On Sept. 27, five men, all British nationals in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran. Police say they found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.
The suspects have since been released on bail .
A dual U.K.-Iranian national was also later arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack. The 25-year-old man was taken into custody in London on Thursday, and on Saturday, Counter Terrorism Policing announced he had been released on bail.
The British government believes Iran "played a part" in the incident at the air base, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America," the prime minister told the BBC.
Iranian officials have said several times since the beginning of the war that any bases used to attack the country would be considered legitimate targets. But the Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement last week that the regime "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran" to the incident.
Frank  Andrews and Tucker  Reals contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: What to Know About the Medical Plane That Went Missing Near Nantucket
articles.title_zh: What to Know About the Medical Plane That Went Missing Near Nantucket
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Coast Guard on Sunday suspended the search for six people in a medical jet that went missing near Nantucket, Massachusetts, a day after debris from the plane was found.
Search and rescue crews operated for approximately 66 hours to locate four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals on the plane that was traveling to Boston from Bermuda early Saturday morning, according to the U.S. Coast Guard.
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard. Their next of kin have been notified, the Coast Guard said.
Earlier, the Coast Guard confirmed that a debris field belonging to the missing Gulfstream G-100 was found Saturday night. The search for the missing passengers continued overnight off the coast of Nantucket, according to the Coast Guard's Northeast District , and spanned 4,445 miles before it was suspended.
The Coast Guard outlined the extensive assets involved in the search, including an HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane, an HC-130 Hercules airplane, an MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter, a 47-foot Motor Lifeboat and the FRC William Sparling, a Sentinel-class fast response cutter.
"Suspending a search is not an easy decision," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, Commander of the Northeast District, said in a statement. "We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts."
The plane took off from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at about 11:40 p.m. ET on Friday, according to data from FlightAware . It went missing after about 1 hour and 45 minutes in the air. FlightAware data show it quickly dropped from about 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet before losing contact. It had been set to land at Boston's Logan International Airport at about 1:30 a.m. local time.
The Federal Aviation Administration confirmed it had lost contact with the plane around 1 a.m. local time Saturday and issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice for the Gulfstream.
Canada's foreign policy department said it was "deeply concerned by the disappearance" of the plane in a statement Sunday.
"Our thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones," the statement said. "We thank the U.S. Coast Guard and all those involved in the search for their tireless efforts."
Officials haven't been able to identify the aircraft components found among the debris, said Kastriot Kastrati, coordinator of the Coast Guard's search and rescue mission, at a briefing Sunday.
"It's very difficult at this point to identify exactly what those components are," he said. "The debris that we have recovered, we've safeguarded and kept for future investigative efforts."
The National Transportation Safety Board told CBS News on Sunday that it is monitoring the situation.
"My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time," Steve MacKinnon, Canada's minister of transport, said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Shooting in Vienna, Ga., Leaves 2 Dead and Dozens Wounded
articles.title_zh: Shooting in Vienna, Ga., Leaves 2 Dead and Dozens Wounded
articles.content_orig:
Rick Jackson and Keisha Lance Bottoms
ATLANTA - The candidates vying to be Georgia's next governor are offering their condolences to the families of those killed and injured in a mass shooting in South Georgia early Sunday morning.
The gunfire erupted shortly after 1:25 a.m. in the historic small city of Vienna, located about 130 miles south of Atlanta, as it celebrated an unofficial homecoming block party at the Dooly County recreation center, coinciding with high school homecoming festivities.
Deputies who heard the noise rushed toward the sound of gunfire.
A total of 35 people were transported to the hospital, but police did not have a clear number of how many were shot. Two men, ages 20 and 23, died.
This shooting comes a week after 12 teens were wounded in a shooting during a birthday party at a park in Macon.
The two incidents are likely to come up this week as Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson continue on the campaign trail.
Republican businessman Rick Jackson released the following statement:
"The news coming out of Vienna is horrific. Please join us in keeping the victims and their loved ones in your prayers, as well as the entire community.
"Our prayers are with the survivors for a full recovery, and with law enforcement and first responders working to find who did this and keep Dooly County safe."
The former Democratic mayor of Atlanta released this statement:
"I am heartbroken by the tragedy in Vienna and the lives taken by senseless gun violence. It is devastating that Georgians are grieving victims of gun violence, just days after the horrific mass shooting at Carolyn Crayton Park in Macon.
"My prayers are with all of the families who have been impacted and for the full recovery of those who were injured.
"I am grateful to the first responders in Dooly County and the GBI, who are working to keep the community safe.
"No family should have to endure this nightmare, and no community should have to live with the fear that a gathering of friends can turn into tragedy."
The investigation into both shootings is continuing.
Bottoms and Jackson are reportedly scheduled to meet for their first and only agreed-to debate on Tuesday.
The Source: The information in this story was gathered from local law enforcement and emergency responders, who provided details regarding the incident and hospital transports, as well as statements released by candidates Rick Jackson and Keisha Lance Bottoms.

articles.title_orig: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Trump defiant about midterm chances as he rallies for Republicans in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has continued rallying for Republican candidates while visiting Ohio, proposing a defiant outlook on his party’s chances in the November 3 midterm elections.
Trump told a rally in Vandalia, Ohio, that he believes there will be a “big surprise” in the upcoming elections, claiming his Democratic opponents do not know what is happening.
Polls have suggested that Democrats could gain ground in the midterms, but the US president said Republicans would do better than critics expect.
“Just get out and vote,” Trump said as he rallied for US Senator Jon Husted, gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and other Republicans.
“If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big,” he said.
Multiple incumbent Republican senators across the country face tough political headwinds, with Trump’s popularity falling in recent months as higher petrol prices and those for other staples persist amid the US-Israel war ⁠⁠on Iran.
Husted, a Republican in a competitive Ohio race against Democrat Sherrod Brown, hopes the president can motivate supporters who might otherwise skip midterm elections.
Trump garnered more than 55 percent of the Ohio vote in the 2024 presidential election, but economic concerns since then have sunk his approval ratings.
Ohio petrol prices increased 35 percent over the past year to $4.16 per gallon (3.8 litres) on average, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which compiles data ⁠⁠on automobile travel. Trump’s trade policy with Canada has also led to retaliatory Canadian tariffs that affect about $3bn worth of Ohio exports, based ⁠⁠on 2025 figures, Canadian broadcaster CBC reported.
Talking to reporters shortly before addressing Saturday’s rally, Husted said the US has to win the Iran war “on our terms” and, in the interim, he is “showing people that I’m fighting for lower prices”.
Trump extensively promoted his administration’s action on data centres, mainly those built for AI, during the rally, saying he was seeking to ensure they “benefit local communities” and praising Husted for an unsuccessful attempt to push forward legislation on the issue.
“Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China,” he said, repeating his defence of data centres.
Data centres have become a hot political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.
The issue became especially acute in Ohio, where Husted has been repeatedly attacked for his role in attracting data centres to the Midwestern state as lieutenant governor.
The Republican-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this past week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats.
“Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centres in Ohio,” Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump’s visit. “Now, he’s making Ohioans foot the bill.”

articles.title_orig: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
articles.title_zh: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
articles.content_orig:
The right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating the incumbent left-wing President Lula da Silva. But he did not obtain more than 50% of the votes required to win outright.
There will be a run-off vote between these two candidates on 25 October.
Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of the former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup attempt after losing the last election.
The election was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With 98.81% of the votes counted, Bolsonaro had 47.24% to Lula's 44.91% of the vote.
Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other presidential candidates who were knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.
The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America's largest country and economy – will follow suit or not.
After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned that the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".
Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".
Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters.
Lula is more popular in Brazil's poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.
He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil's history.
After that election, Bolsonaro's supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023.
Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro's wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday.
Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the January 8th riots, amnesty if elected.
He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.
The president of Brazil's supreme electoral court said on Sunday that no evidence of international interference was found in the election.
During the campaign, President Lula made "sovereignty" a key pillar of his campaign and at times accused the United States of trying to interfere in and influence Brazil's elections. He has pledged to increase defence spending.
Earlier this year, Flávio Bolsonaro successfully lobbied the United States to designate the two biggest Brazilian gangs as terrorist organisations.
In July, Brazil refused visas for two US State Department officials who Brazil alleged were attempting to sow doubt in Brazil's electoral system, which the US called "baseless." It came after Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly told a group of foreign diplomats that Brazil's voting machines share the same origin as Venezuela's, which is false.
Last year, Donald Trump used the coup trial of Jair Bolsonaro as justification for imposing tariffs on Brazil and sanctioning some top officials and judges.
A win for Flávio Bolsonaro would likely see Brazil join the US's "Shield of Americas" coalition against narco-trafficking and align more closely with the US.
Bolsonaro has pledged though to maintain an "economically pragmatic" relationship with China, which has overtaken the US as Brazil's biggest trading partner and is a crucial customer for Brazil's soy and beef exports.
Corruption became a key issue in this campaign after a scandal involving a jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiled senior figures across the political spectrum.
Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged that he'd asked Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).
Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to the Supreme Court judge Alexandre de Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing.
Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.
Crime and insecurity were also top concerns for voters. Brazil's homicide rate has fallen, but street crime such as phone thefts, that are highly visible to voters, have increased - and violence and drug trafficking are still major problems.
Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to designate Brazilian gangs as terrorists and build maximum-security prisons akin to those in El Salvador. His father, during his presidency, loosened gun ownership restrictions.
Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but has launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons.
The economy has been central to this campaign, too: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth.
Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, mostly notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty.
He has backed more investment in data centres and rare earth minerals, which Brazil is rich in, with strong state involvement to ensure that Brazil benefits.
He has also backed oil drilling exploration near the mouth of the Amazon River, which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro's presidency.
Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.

articles.title_orig: Rescuers suspend search for survivors after plane went missing off US coast
articles.title_zh: Rescuers suspend search for survivors after plane went missing off US coast
articles.content_orig:
US authorities have suspended the search for six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston.
The Coast Guard said on Sunday evening it was ending the search off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, after 66 hours of looking for the passengers.
"We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones," the Coast Guard said on Sunday.
The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT). Authorities have notified the next of kin of those on the flight, four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals.
Authorities had said earlier that they had located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft on Saturday evening.
The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).
According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.
Among those on board were two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.
The crew flew to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, who are not Canadian, Togeretz said.
FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).
Radio transmissions shows trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.
"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?," the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"
The pilot's response was inaudible.
"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.
The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.
An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".
The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".

articles.title_orig: Russia hits Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits Ukraine’s capital
articles.title_zh: Russia hits Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits Ukraine’s capital
articles.content_orig:
Putin accuses Europe of escalating tensions over Russia’s war on Ukraine
Russia has struck a key bridge in Kyiv just as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital to meet President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The unannounced visit, marked by the sound of air sirens and explosions, came on Sunday to underscore Germany’s support for the nation at a time when Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities are increasing.
In a written statement, Merz said he “travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks”.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Merz and Zelenskyy met at the National Academy of Sciences, which was struck by a Russian drone on September 28.
Zelenskyy told Merz that Kyiv’s citizens are going through “terrible nights and days” due to the ongoing Russian attacks.
Merz was accompanied by his economy minister, as well as executives from several large German companies, such as Siemens Energy and Diehl Defence.
Ukraine and Germany are also expected to finalise a deal to produce drones and other weapons together that can travel more than 600 miles (965.6km) in an effort to strike deeper into Russia.
Germany has been one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters. In April, the two countries signed a military pact worth more than $4bn. On Sunday, a $1.1bn military aid package is set to be announced, alongside $394m to repair damage to Ukraine’s energy sector.
Merz’s visit comes a day after Russia warned foreign diplomats and nationals to leave the capital to avoid getting hurt.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence promised to intensify strikes on Ukraine after Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Reuters news agency that it is doubling down on targeting Russian oil refineries after several civilians were killed and wounded over the weekend.
The strike that hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Sunday also damaged a road and the supply of hot water in the area, according to a social media statement from Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. It is the second bridge in the capital to be hit this weekend.
Russia’s all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year. Both sides have increased the number of drone and missile attacks on infrastructure, logistics and military sites in recent months.

articles.title_orig: Trump announces members of ‘Super Intelligence Force’ to coordinate AI policy
articles.title_zh: Trump announces members of ‘Super Intelligence Force’ to coordinate AI policy
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump announced the formation of an artificial intelligence task force Sunday, naming National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to lead it.
The other members of the group include Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael. The task force, Trump said, will report to him and to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
“Following the Historic White House Accord on Super Intelligence, where the World’s most important Technology Companies came together, and confirmed their responsibilities to the American People, I am announcing the formation of the Super Intelligence Force,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Trump on Tuesday met with tech leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. Clayton was also at the meeting. The summit came after AI leaders issued existential warnings surrounding the technology, which Trump has largely downplayed.
Tech leaders have called on Washington to regulate the industry, which he has said he will not do. Last week, after the summit, Trump said the leaders had reached what appeared to be a nonbinding agreement of “tremendous self-regulation.”
“The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government’s engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies,” Trump added to his Truth Social post Sunday.
NBC News reported Friday that Trump was expected to name Clayton AI czar. Before he took over as director of national intelligence, Clayton was U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York and chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Venture capitalist David Sacks had been AI czar, before he had to step down when his term as a special government employee expired.
Trump announced last month that he would create an AI task force as the issue has become a flashpoint in Washington and beyond, with some lawmakers calling for a laissez-faire approach, while others have advocated for action to be taken. Some politicians perceived as 2028 hopefuls, such as Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, have sought to regulate the technology at the state level.
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.title_zh: How was Flydubai co-pilot cleared despite being deemed a security risk?
articles.content_orig:
A Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain with an emergency axe and attempting to seize control of the flight bound for Israel had previously been barred from flying over concerns about alleged “extremist” views, raising questions about how he was allowed to fly to Tel Aviv.
The co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, according to multiple media reports.
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has described the September 30 incident aboard Flight FZ1073 as an attempted “terrorist” operation .
But investigators are still working to establish the motive and whether anyone else was connected to the attack, which has raised concerns about pilot vetting and aviation security.
So, what security checks do pilots have to go through and how al-Hammami may have evaded background checks?
That is now one of the central questions facing investigators.
Al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman because of concerns that he had adopted “extremist” views and was instead moved to an administrative role at Oman Air, according to sources who spoke to the AP news agency.
He was subsequently hired by Flydubai.
A Gulf diplomat told AP that al-Hammami had undergone standard security checks before being hired. It wasn’t immediately clear to what extent the co-pilot was vetted.
The US-based network CNN reported that a LinkedIn profile bearing al-Hammami’s name said he had spent seven years at Oman Air before leaving in February 2025. The profile said he joined Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and left in January this year.
It is unclear what those alleged views were or whether Oman informed other countries or airlines about its concerns.
Background checks for commercial pilots vary by airline and country, with no single global standard governing the process, an airline pilot and instructor told Al Jazeera.
The captain with an international airline who chose to remain anonymous said pilots are generally required to obtain aviation medical certification from the regulator in the country where they are licensed to fly.
In the UAE, that is overseen by the General Civil Aviation Authority (GCAA), he said.
Some airlines also require prospective pilots to provide police clearance certificates from their country of residence as part of pre-employment screening, the pilot added.
One type of check is a Class 1 medical assessment, which typically examines areas including vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, as well as conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.
When it comes to security checks, aviation rules require background checks for personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.
Psychological assessments, drug and alcohol testing and other evaluations may be required depending on the jurisdiction.
Israel has some of the world’s toughest aviation security measures.
As a result, questions have been raised over how the alleged attacker was allowed to operate a flight to Israel, despite reportedly being an Omani national and Oman having no diplomatic relations with Israel.
According to the Haaretz newspaper, Israeli authorities received the Flydubai flight’s crew and passenger lists before it departed. Under a law passed in 2023, airlines are required to provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, to Israel up to 48 hours before a flight.
The Israel Tax Authority confirmed to Haaretz that it had received the lists for the Flydubai flight. The media outlet reported that the information is also supposed to be available to Israeli security bodies, including the Mossad, police and Shin Bet, to identify people who may pose a security risk.
According to security sources who spoke to Haaretz, the Transportation Ministry’s Security Department and the Mossad are responsible for checking foreign flight crews and issuing alerts if concerns arise.
However, two security sources told Haaretz that while the Transportation Ministry holds responsibility “on paper”, it does not have its own intelligence capacity.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel has longstanding arrangements with foreign airlines aimed at preventing pilots who are nationals of countries without diplomatic relations with Israel from flying there.
Netanyahu has described what happened as a “loophole” and Israel says it will now strengthen its checks.
The UAE has not yet publicly established a motive or announced whether investigators believe al-Hammami acted alone.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said on Saturday that the latest ‘terrorist’ attack is a new warning that the region’s fight against “extremism” is not over.
“This underscores the importance of the UAE’s early and firm stance: no tolerance for extremism and no leniency towards its rhetoric. Security begins with confronting hatred and drying up the sources of extremism,” he posted on X.

articles.title_orig: Bills report card: Josh Allen falters, secondary gets torched by Patriots
articles.title_zh: Bills report card: Josh Allen falters, secondary gets torched by Patriots
articles.content_orig:
The New England Patriots defense faced a tough test against the undefeated Buffalo Bills and resoundingly passed.
All week, the talk was about Josh Allen , and rightfully so. The 2024 MVP was off to another MVP-level start to the season.
Oct 4, 2026; Orchard Park, New York, USA; Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) is pressured by New England Patriots linebacker Gabe Jacas (50) during the third quarter at New Highmark Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark Konezny-Imagn ImagesMark Konezny-Imagn Images
However, against Coach Vrabel 's heavy zone defense on Sunday, Allen was largely held in check thanks to the unit's discipline on the edges. Gabe Jacas and Elijah Ponder were able to collapse the pocket, which helped eliminate his signature quarterback scrambles.
A non-factor with his legs, Allen was limited to just five running attempts for four yards and a touchdown.
With two safeties taking away deep throws down the field, Allen was forced to take underneath throws and sustain long drives to put up points. As a result, Allen had his lowest QBR of the season, 50.3, along with a rookie-mistake interception to Patriots safety Craig Woodson on the Bills' last drive of the game.
On the ground, the Bills superstar was largely held in check. New England's front seven was disciplined on early downs and forced Cook to run between the tackles.
While he eventually finished with 75 yards and a touchdown, the bulk of his production came in the fourth quarter when Buffalo started to use its three-tight-end sets.
For New England's defense, the game plan was simple: set the edge to prevent outside runs and take away deep throws. And while Josh Allen and James Cook had their highlight plays, Mike Vrabel's unit stepped up when it mattered most.
Mike Vrabel's defense answered the bell when the game hung in the balance and proved that its zone scheme can go toe-to-toe with the AFC's best.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
articles.title_zh: U.S. Rushes to Withdraw Bombers From U.K. Air Base After New Threats
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met.
On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room.
Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks.
"The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting.
Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks.
Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces.
A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.
If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war.
Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East.
"The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday.
The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs .
Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday. But prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease the burden on consumers.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel.
— The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Nearly all were rural banks, which âremain the weakest part of the system , with poor asset quality, low capitalization, and governance shortcomings,â Fitch wrote.
After a massive credit expansion drove growth, âthe financial systemâs problems now constrain that growth ,â a Rhodium Group expert told ChinaTalk.

articles.title_orig: FBI arrests alleged Chinese agent at LAX after she allegedly surveilled son of Taiwanese president
articles.title_zh: FBI arrests alleged Chinese agent at LAX after she allegedly surveilled son of Taiwanese president
articles.content_orig:
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News.
Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government.
Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further.
It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney.
A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family.
Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai.
Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips.
"If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint.
Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades . It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured.
CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment.
The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home.
Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening.
CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu.
Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint.
The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account.
"Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote.
The complaint claims  Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security.
Holt's affidavit claims  Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission.
She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint.
On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said.
Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties.
Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications.
Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA , Taiwan's national news agency.
Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S.
Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang , 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent.
Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents.
The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime.
New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China.
In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China.

articles.title_orig: -60 kg: Ahmad Yusifov is Azerbaijan’s New Hero
articles.title_zh: -60 kg: Ahmad Yusifov is Azerbaijan’s New Hero
articles.content_orig:
Judo is always an amazing sport to watch or take part in, one that provides challenge, not just from fighter to fighter, but in our thinking and analysis. This category challenged the established order in Baku, yielding an immensely exciting day of judo.
As the judoka entered the arena, the volume rose ten-fold! Ahmad Yusifov had already given his crowd much to be thankful for and they were determined to continue giving their support right until the end. Sherzod Davlatov, however, had no intention of buckling under the pressure of Yusifov’s home-ground advantage.
Davlatov arrived with a powerful style and a positive attitude. He attacked and attacked and eventually caught Yusifov with a ko-uchi-gari for a waza-ari. This seemed to light a fire under the Azerbaijani fighter and he found a new gear.
Davlatov, not feeling that there had been a change in his opponent, continued to come forward and attempted to pick Yusifov up but he was ready and countered beautifully, scoring his own waza-ari. His transition was also on point and not settling for just an equaliser, Ahmad Yusifov circled and held his opponent for a second waza-ari.
Azerbaijan has their first world champion of these championships, a new hero who won gold as well as the hearts of his nation. After the final he said, “I always tried to keep positive thoughts in my mind and to believe that I could win, especially in front of this crowd. Their support was incredible. Every single person in the arena gave me energy and helped me throughout the competition. I felt that support very strongly and it pushed me to give everything I had. Now I am world champion and I feel great. This title belongs, in part, to everyone who supported me here today.”
What a contest! This 4 minutes had absolutely everything: speed, strength, skill, drama, intensity, acrobatics, courage. There was nothing missing.
As one attacked, the other made split-second decisions to defend or counter. Impressive awareness accompanied every choice and the accumulation of movements created a magnetic contest; it was impossible to turn away. A counter from Nagayama put a yuko on the board after 2 and a half minutes but there was still no indication of who would earn the nod at full time.
Nagayama held his ground, despite looking as though he may have picked up an injury during the later stages of the fight. Bliev could not repeat his bronze medal winning performance of 2025. Nagayama also missed out on a repeat performance but the bronze medal in Baku will certainly be some consolation; two world championship medals in as many years is no easy ask.
Giorgi Sardashvilli had tasted gold in the past and wanted to recreate the feeling of stepping on to the world championship podium. A positive, attacking style led him to do just that in Baku!
He out-attacked Yung Wei Yang, putting him under a great deal of pressure from the outset. As Yang began to collect penalties, Sardalashvili only grew more determined. Yang attempted to adjust but the Georgian had his strategy and a perfect rhythm.
A small chop-down from Sardalashvili created the conditions for some momentum to take hold and he spun Yang on to his back from a position already considered to be ne-waza. There he held him down for ippon. This young Georgian astounded everyone when he won his world title two years ago, but now he is proving that it wasn’t luck but the beginning of an impressive career.

articles.title_orig: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.title_zh: An Invitation From the Prophet to the World
articles.content_orig:
In his closing remarks during the Sunday afternoon session of general conference on October 4, 2026, President Dallin H. Oaks of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints invited the world to participate in the Salt Lake Temple Celebration, either in person or virtually.
As part of his special invitation, President Oaks highlighted a new video series. “Following this session of general conference, the first episode of a dynamic video series, ‘Dedicate,’ will premiere worldwide in multiple languages,” he said. “More will come in the months ahead, including a virtual tour of the Salt Lake Temple.”
“Dedicate” follows seven young adults from Brazil, France, Ghana, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines and the United States as they explore the Salt Lake Temple, meet with Church leaders and navigate questions of faith, purpose and spiritual growth. Throughout the series, they share personal experiences as they deepen their understanding of temples and strengthen their faith in Jesus Christ.
The first episode is now available on the Church’s YouTube channel and will be added to the Gospel Library app in the coming days.
Four additional “Dedicate” episodes will be released every Sunday at 8 a.m. MDT through November 1, with the sixth and final episode set to air in spring 2027. In addition to English, episodes are available in Cantonese, Chinese (Traditional), French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish.
For the first time since 1893, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will open the doors of the newly renovated Salt Lake Temple. The public is invited to experience the beauty of this sacred space from April 5, 2027, to October 1, 2027. This significant six-month event is for everyone, whether they participate in person on Temple Square or from elsewhere in the world through virtual experiences.
The celebration will include the open house tour, exhibits, performances, films, service opportunities, and other experiences centered on the Savior of the world. During the celebration, guests will also find opportunities to enjoy live music, exhibits, and other events. Learn more and reserve tickets for tours at TempleSquare.org or download the Temple Square app.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Ivy League school’s president promises action after woman alleged she was drugged ⁠and raped by fraternity members
Cornell University will examine the role of fraternities and sororities on campus after an outcry over the school’s handling ⁠of a student’s rape allegations, the Ivy League school’s president has said.
A civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman , who ⁠alleges she was drugged ⁠and raped in ​2024 by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity, has prompted outrage and soul-searching at Cornell over its campus culture at the ⁠school in Ithaca, New York.
In a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
“At ​their best, these organisations can provide ‌students with friendship, belonging, mentorship ‌and a powerful sense of community,” he said. “But being part of a group can never diminish ‌individual responsibility.“
The university would seek input, he said, from students, alumni and others on how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of others”.
The lawsuit against Cornell, seven fraternity members and others, alleges that the school failed to adequately punish ‌some of the accused students.
The accused men have denied all wrongdoing, the New York Times has reported.
Cornell has defended its handling of the matter, saying that in 2024 it launched ​a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity from campus. The school said it also imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.
But “we must do better”, Kotlikoff said, adding: “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
He vowed that ⁠university officials would “be more transparent” about their actions related to the 2024 incident, but ​he did not detail ​specific initiatives that the university would take. “In ​the coming weeks, we will create additional opportunities for members of our ​community to ask ‌questions and hear directly ​from university leadership,” ​he said.
The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.
As the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York attorney general, investigates, new attention has been drawn to the findings of a state-mandated sexual violence survey conducted by Cornell in 2025, which found that 35% of female undergraduates who completed the survey reported that they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact while at the university.
The 2025 version of the survey was the first to specifically include unwanted choking or strangulation in the definition of nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation that students were asked about, in addition to nonconsensual penetration and/or sexual touching.
Guardian staff contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.title_zh: Why even resilient forests are struggling to regrow after wildfires
articles.content_orig:
Kim Desiato, a firefighter from Tucson, Arizona, stops to look for hot spots in the aftermath of the Lewis Lake Fire in Yellowstone National Park in August 1988. The fire forced the closure of the south entrance to the park.
(CNN) — As Monica Turner trekked across the western hills of Yellowstone National Park, the cold rain was inescapable. Even the constant movement of putting one foot in front of the other as she fought through a slew of dense branches could not warm her body. It was easy to forget it was July.
Four years later in 2017, Turner made the same journey. But instead of fighting the once compact forest, she was met with a desolate clearing as the sun pounded above her. After the Maple Fire the year before, all that was left of the towering trees was a smattering of survivors looking over a sea of skinny, pencil-like sticks sprouting from the charred dirt.
In Turner’s time as a researcher, she has seen massive destruction and its subsequent regrowth as she studied the impacts of Yellowstone’s 1988 fires, which left a crown jewel of the national park system scorched. This made the level of destruction Turner witnessed in 2017 even more shocking — especially as the area had burned before without this level of loss.
Researchers across the US are seeing a similar trend — forests that are historically adapted to fire are now often being obliterated by the fast-moving, high temperature wildfires that are becoming increasingly more common with climate change . These researchers are grappling with what it will mean for our world if the trees that are the centerpiece of these landscapes we love don’t recover like they once did.
The fire itself is not inherently the problem. Every scientist CNN spoke with emphasized the need for fire on the landscapes they researched. But the lack of prescribed burning, a practice long used by indigenous people to clear out dead plants and to keep landscapes healthy, has left these trees vulnerable . It means their futures — when they encounter hotter, more vicious fires — are uncertain.
As these ecologies start to shift, it’s unclear if or when these different areas around the US will hit a tipping point where the trees won’t come back. Instead, researchers say it’s more likely there will be a gradual conversion over time, with once towering forests becoming robust scrublands or large fields of grassland.
Here’s how some places around the country are changing, and how one state is succeeding in preserving its native wildlife.
As Turner stood on the dirt field, the air was hot — much hotter than during her previous 2013 visit. Cool summers and rain had been the norm for Yellowstone during her years of research. The heat was so intense this time that a field assistant was hospitalized for dehydration during the trip, said Turner, who works at the University of Wisconsin-Madison as the Eugene P. Odum Professor of Ecology and a Vilas Research Professor.
The ash coating the former forest floor reminded her of the ash she walked through during the 1988 fires — ash that covered her face and caked her socks. For a long time, Turner thought the wildfires from that summer 38 years ago represented how forests could and would recover. Despite miles of charred trees, the research in her field showed the forest would come back, and with a high density of trees, she said. But Turner said she didn’t appreciate “how much things could change in a relatively short time.”
“We could see what we call ghost logs, which is where there had been large logs on the ground, and they were completely combusted,” she said. “And then you can see their shadows where the white ash is left behind from the hot temperatures.”
Only about 5 percent of the tree seedlings have grown back so far from the 2016 fire, compared to what burned. In place of the trees, grasses blow in the exposed meadow, now dotted with wildflowers that commonly sprout after a wildfire. Turner said she is seeing “a slow but detectable shift” to plants that are “more tolerant of warmer, drier conditions” and can grow back more easily if more wildfires come.
Slowly but surely, these changes could impact visitors to the park, Turner said. People like trees, for both how they look and the practical element of shade during hikes, she said, and the changes the forest is undergoing could impact how and when people visit the park.
The repercussions are seen in more unexpected ways as well — at one point, the park had a temporary ban on fishing, including catch and release, because the fish were already too stressed out from low water levels and the high water temperatures that were partially due to the lack of shade, she said.
“What will be the consequences for lots of other values that people care about in that region?” Turner said. “That could be wildlife habitat. It could be water availability. It could be shade if you’re hiking.”
But ultimately, it’s not yet clear what the future Yellowstone will look like.
About 100 miles northeast of California’s state capital, Derek Young stood in the middle of a clearing in Plumas National Forest. The carcasses of burnt trees that surrounded him felt like a graveyard, the remains left in the wake of the 2021 Dixie Fire.
An occasional bird would chirp in the distance, but the forest emanated an eerie stillness, said Young, a research ecologist at the University of California, Davis. Fifteen years ago, Young started studying these landscapes as a PhD student. Many of them are now unrecognizable compared to the thriving forests they once were.
“It’s really actually crazy to how much change has happened,” he said.
Many of the areas Young studies are changing from dazzling emerald trees to fields of shrubs — even years after the wildfires.
The shrubs, ranging from deer brush to white thorn shrub, are incredibly good at resprouting, Young said. While fire might lop off the shrub tops, their roots remain, helping the plants return quickly, he said. It’s stiff competition for trees to endure, which need specific conditions to grow back compared to the hardy, drought-tolerant shrubs, he said.
In just a few years, the shrubs can grow to be as tall as a person, covering the entirety of an area, Young said. “It can really feel like you’re swimming in a sea of shrubs. You can’t see more than a few feet ahead of you.”
There are a couple of factors required for trees to successfully reemerge. Some species of trees can grow in the shade, but those species are also more likely to be destroyed during a high temperature fire, he said. Others need the heat of a fire to release their seeds, while many others don’t, Young said. Those seeds then need to land in an area where they can grow and survive, which can be impacted by wind and wildlife, he added. A lot needs to happen in a short window of time in order for them to regrow.
As he sees these landscapes shift, it’s hard to weigh if this is inherently a bad change — although he noted the important services forests currently provide humans, namely capturing and holding carbon dioxide through carbon sequestration.
“As forests burn up, they release carbon, contribute to climate change, which makes it more likely for more fires to burn and convert more forests,” he said. “You could say, if you care about humanity’s well-being, that that’s actually a reason to favor maintenance and restoration of forests in place of post-fire shrub fields.”
“I do sometimes try to think from the perspective of like, what if there were no humans, and there is no society to decide what our values are,” he said. “In that scenario, I think the sort of definitive answer is the most valuable ecosystem is the one that is adapted to the site in the absence of all the human intervention.”
But he notes this change to shrubs is not happening in that theoretical vacuum without humans.
“It’s not that the system naturally wanted to be shrubs. We created that condition by suppressing fires for 100 years,” he said.
