articles.title_orig: Saudi-Backed Yemen Forces Begin Operation to Retake Houthi Areas
articles.title_zh: Saudi-Backed Yemen Forces Begin Operation to Retake Houthi Areas
articles.content_orig:
The announcement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis reportedly cut a vital supply route to besieged city of Taiz
Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis , even as the militant group made fresh gains on the ground, reportedly encircling a government-held city.
Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a statement on Sunday: “I announce today the start of military operations to retake the remaining territories of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory.”
The announcement sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia . The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title_orig: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.title_zh: Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans
articles.content_orig:
Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations.
Like the broader electorate , Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living.
There are clear signs his party is paying the price.
A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question.
Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%.
That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election.
Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference.
The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country.
The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections.
Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.”
“What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.”
But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012.
“Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said.
Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling.
His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference.
Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it.
Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue.
Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters.
A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024.
Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues.
“It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.”
“I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added.
Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family.
While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies.
Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough.
While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S.
Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans.
“There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added.
In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.
Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE.
Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics.
She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.”
“They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added.
The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street’s AI Party Is on Edge as Soaring Yields Raise Risks
articles.title_zh: Wall Street’s AI Party Is on Edge as Soaring Yields Raise Risks
articles.content_orig:
Bonds are in a serious slump. Over the third quarter, fixed income markets sold off sharply as concerns about sticky inflation, oil price spikes and heavy corporate borrowing to fund the artificial intelligence buildout put upward pressure on yields.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury hit 5.26% and the yield on the 30-year hit 5.59% just this week—their highest levels since the financial crisis—as the selloff intensified. Bond yields move inversely with prices. Even escalating Treasury buybacks weren’t enough to calm bond investors’ nerves.
“Year-to-date yield moves up have been substantial,” says Dominic Pappalardo, chief multi-asset strategist for Morningstar Wealth. “They’ve been driven mostly by inflation concerns.”
Those rising yields came against the backdrop of anxiety over unsustainable fiscal deficits and an economy that’s still running hot despite rising rates. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates for the first time in more than three years, and investors expect at least one more hike for the remainder of the year.
The Morningstar US Core Bond Index fell 3.35% over the third quarter. Long-term Treasury bonds fared worst, losing 7.65%. That makes sense; long-dated bonds tend to have longer durations, making their prices more sensitive to interest rates. As rates soared this year, longer-term bonds sold off more than short-term ones, fueled by worries about uncertain fiscal policy and stubborn inflation. Short-term core bonds fared best, with losses of 0.89%. High-yield bonds, which tend to have shorter durations and are less sensitive to rate fluctuations, lost 1.71%.
Looming large for the bond market is the booming issuance of debt related to the artificial intelligence buildout, as mega-cap tech firms borrow billions to fund data centers and other infrastructure.
A recent estimate from Goldman Sachs suggests debt issuance from hyperscalers could reach $420 billion in 2027. That would represent an increase of more than 60% from 2026, their analysts say. So far this year, they find that hyperscaler firms have issued $229 billion in debt.
“A new dynamic is changing the composition of the credit markets,” says Morningstar Wealth’s Pappalardo. He notes that concentration risk —a familiar phenomenon in equities markets—could come into play if the trend continues. If the share of hyperscaler debt in fixed-income markets continues to increase, “that concentration problem will become concerning at some point.”
Pappalardo says he isn’t seeing signs of bond market concentration yet, but that it’s worth keeping an eye on. Earlier this year, he says AI-related debt accounted for about 15% of the corporate bond universe .
The Fed raised interest rates at its September meeting for the first time in more than three years, bringing the federal-funds target to a range of 3.75%-4.00%. The move pushed up yields on both short- and long-term bonds as the market priced in expectations of persistent inflation and a higher rate environment in the months and years ahead.
Inflationary pressures are clearly top of mind for policymakers. The war in Iran is driving up oil prices and energy costs. At the same time, the AI boom appears to be raising costs elsewhere in the economy.
After the September decision, analysts quickly turned their attention to the Fed’s next move. “It’s rare that they only hike once,” Morningstar Wealth’s Pappalardo says. And some analysts argue that with other measures of economic health (like employment and business activity) looking robust, the central bank has plenty of reasons to keep raising interest rates to prevent overheating. As of this writing, bond futures markets are pricing in more than 50% odds that the Fed hikes twice before the end of the year. That would bring the federal-funds target rate to a range of 4.25%-4.50%.
Analysts agree it’s unlikely that yields will drop significantly anytime soon. Inflation is still sticky, which has ramifications for both longer-dated bonds and yields across the board. Pappalardo says the outlook for bonds depends on two key questions: “How high will rates go from here, and what will bring them back down?”
Pappalardo says that with elevated energy prices from the Iran war keeping inflation above target, it’s reasonable to expect yields to remain high for some time. More Fed hikes are on the table, too. On the other hand, resolving tensions in the Middle East could ease the pressure and help rates fall. “You would expect energy prices to start to work their way back lower, taking the top off inflation and pushing it closer to the 2% target,” he says.
Some analysts have argued that markets should get used to a new paradigm of higher yields after two decades of rock-bottom levels. Going forward, 10-year yields of 4%, 5%, or even higher might not be all that abnormal. “We’re in a different era,” characterized by larger-scale fiscal spending, higher inflation, and higher growth, according to Sebastien Mallet, manager of the $313 million T. Rowe Price Global Value Equity TRGVX .
But it’s not all bad news for investors. Strategists emphasize that, while painful on paper, higher yields also mean more income for bond investors , as well as a bigger cushion to offset price declines.

articles.title_orig: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.title_zh: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force withdrew all of its B-1 bombers stationed at an air base in southern England that is used by American military forces to strike Iran after an investigation discovered a planned terror attack, The Associated Press reported Sunday.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the United States, AP reported, citing a Pentagon official who was not authorized to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on condition of anonymity.
Aviation watchers such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance and others have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war, AP said. These observers saw many B-1 bombers take off from the base on Sunday.
A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, authorities took six individuals into custody and later released them on bail during the investigation.
British authorities have linked the terror plot to Tehran, although Iran has denied involvement.
RAF Fairford is located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London and has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
At least two vessels were struck over the weekend in waters near Oman and Iran , the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre reported, as Tehran reiterated its position on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen unless its conditions for ending the war with the U.S. are met.
On Saturday, the UKMTO, a British maritime security alert service, said it received a report of a crude oil tanker being hit by an unknown projectile four nautical miles east of Oman. It said another tanker was reported as being similarly struck Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz, causing damage to its engine room.
Attacks on shipping in the strait, through which about a fifth of the world's oil supplies moved before the start of the U.S. and Israel-led war on Feb. 28, have been happening on a regular basis for weeks.
"The Strait of Hormuz will not open until Iran's seven conditions based on the Islamabad Memorandum are met, and Iran will not regulate its national security with tweets from American officials," Iranian state media agency Nour News quoted Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf as saying Sunday.
President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed an interim deal in June, known as the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, that resulted in a brief hiatus in fighting.
Tehran's conditions for allowing ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz include a halt to U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets.
A key demand of the U.S. has been that Iran dismantle its nuclear weapons program.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure reportedly came under renewed attacks.
Reuters reported Saturday that Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had targeted a facility owned by Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco in the capital Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones. The group said the attack was in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen's Sanaa and other provinces.
A large plume of smoke and fire rose above the facility, Reuters quoted a witness as saying.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported attack. Aramco did not immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request for comment.
If confirmed, it would be the latest escalation in what has effectively become a second front in the Iran war.
Some investors say they expect full-scale fighting to resume in the Middle East.
"The situation is fluid and volatile. To me, as we are developing and looking at the situation, it's not a question of if, but when the conflict resumes full force," Bader Al-Saif, founding president of Al-Saif Consulting, told CNBC's Access Middle East show on Friday.
The ongoing attacks and prospect of a further escalation have driven energy prices higher in recent weeks, raising inflation expectations globally and putting upward pressure on government borrowing costs .
Reports that the U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, along with an amphibious force carrying 2,000 Marines, pushed crude oil prices higher on Thursday. But prices edged lower Friday, after the Group of Seven nations announced the release of diesel and crude stocks to ease the burden on consumers.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 6 cents to close at $102.25 per barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude shed $1.76 to settle at $91.11 per barrel.
— The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: More than 1,200 Colorado students have earned a climate ‘seal’: ‘We’re the ones growing up in this world’
articles.title_zh: More than 1,200 Colorado students have earned a climate ‘seal’: ‘We’re the ones growing up in this world’
articles.content_orig:
A statewide initiative pairs climate-focused coursework with community service – and is spreading to other states
As a student at a high school not far from Denver’s main airport, Anthony Muñoz wondered whether the jet fuel from airplanes flying above his campus was harming living things.
An avid gardener, Muñoz partnered with a local university to create a garden on the campus of his charter school, Vista Academy, filling it with native plants that could detect ground-level ozone pollution. He also worked with climate scientists from the National Center for Atmospheric Research, a federal office in nearby Boulder, who directed Muñoz on what data to collect, what the condition of leaves reveals about air quality and why milkweed matters for monarch butterfly migration.
“One garden’s a very good data source,” said Muñoz. “Colorado’s so beautiful, and I would hate to see it wilt away.”
Muñoz built the “ozone garden” for his capstone project as part of Colorado’s seal of climate literacy, a statewide initiative that pairs climate-focused coursework with hands-on community service. To earn the seal – an endorsement on high school diplomas and transcripts – students must complete at least two advanced courses that cover the Earth’s climate systems and an approved project that tackles a climate issue in their community.
Since 2024, when Colorado lawmakers approved the seal, 26 of the state’s 179 school districts have adopted it, according to Lyra Colorado, an education non-profit that advocates for the seal. Now, the model is spreading to other states. Maine adopted its own climate seal earlier this year, and California just signed into law a bill to establish the seal for graduates there. Youth coalitions have pushed for the policy in Hawaii and Minnesota, with varying success.
Proponents of the seal argue that young people must understand and combat the climate crisis, without waiting for political leaders to reach consensus on how it should be taught. They also hope the endorsement will connect students to a rapidly expanding green workforce, preparing them to work on solar grids and climate-resilient farms or in water resource management and urban heat mitigation. And, as climate change begins to alter almost every aspect of human life, the seal could offer anxious teenagers a sense of agency and ability to make some difference.
“Where we can make the most difference is often in our local community,” said Laura Schifter, a senior fellow with the Aspen Institute’s This Is Planet Ed, a climate education group. She said the seal offers students a chance to learn about the climate crisis, a topic rarely covered in depth in K-12 classrooms, and called it “a really promising policy”.
Still, the seal has faced hurdles, including tight school district budgets, concern about new burdens on schools and the federal government’s attempts to refute climate science.
The idea for the seal originated with Lyra Colorado, the non-profit in Denver that supports community-based education programs. Rural students and educators the group was working with on another climate-related project said they wanted a way to explore climate change as a reality in their daily lives, not just through a dense unit in a textbook, according to Mary Seawell, Lyra’s CEO.
To earn the seal, students need to complete two classes that promote “ climate literacy ”, or basic principles of the climate crisis, such as its causes and how to mitigate it. One of them must be a science class, such as environmental studies, biology or earth science. The other course can be in any discipline, including the humanities or fine arts. For example, this year Denver public schools will build lessons about climate change into its state-mandated civics course, Seawell said. Student projects for the seal have addressed beaver dams, building trails, snow science and forestry management.
An estimated 1,200 students have received the seal so far, said Seawell.
Funding, though, has been a challenge: state lawmakers provided less than $20,000 for the seal’s rollout. Many students fund their projects out of pocket or, like Muñoz, secure grants: he co-wrote a $1m grant proposal to the city to pay for the gardens at his school. Lyra created its own grant program to help local schools pay for teachers’ time, student projects and even graduation cords.
Muñoz, now a sophomore studying mechanical engineering at the Colorado School of Mines, said the seal allowed him to learn climate leadership skills. He’s currently vice-president of the college’s environmental club and tries to inspire his peers to take action.
“Are you going to think beyond yourself and help not only those in need but the environment, or will you sit back and wait for someone else to change the world for you?” he said.
As more students like Muñoz graduate with the seal, many have started to work on climate issues at their colleges and in new states.
Rylan Neumann graduated last year from the Boulder Valley school district, enrolling that fall at the University of California, Berkeley, to study environmental economics. Almost immediately, she joined an eco-club and boarded a train to Sacramento, where she lobbied state lawmakers in support of the state’s pending climate seal bill.
“Getting more students involved in climate action and how they’ll be impacted in the future is essential,” she said. “We’re the ones growing up in this world.”
In Hawaii, a student member of the state board of education championed the endorsement for high schools on the islands. The Minnesota Youth Council, a state advisory board with representatives from middle and high schools, recommended the seal during this year’s legislative session.
State education officials in Maine, meanwhile, adopted the seal directly to avoid legislative debate.
“Students want to be involved in climate action, in environmental literacy, in green careers,” said Teddy Lyman, a K-12 climate education specialist in Maine. “They’re often doing the work already but don’t have the recognition. They didn’t see a sort of pathway to continue that work and embark on that as a potential career.”
During a spring pilot across nine high schools, Lyman expected roughly a dozen students to apply for the seal. Instead, he said, nearly 57 seniors did.
Melissa Luetje teaches science at Freeport high school, which enrolls about 600 students near Casco Bay. Warming and rising sea levels have eroded coastal infrastructure and flooded surface streets.
For a seal-approved class she teaches on research, students will monitor woodlands for insect damage, develop new ways to compost or commodify an invasive crab species, and work on a sustainable fishery.
“How climate impacts the coastal community is very different from the interior or a city,” Luetje said. “It’s up to each community to figure out what they value and how they want to roll this out.”
As the seal expands, proponents have tried to connect the high school endorsement directly to green workforce pipelines.
Lyra Colorado has started working with higher education institutions like Colorado Mountain College to align it with certification in the skilled trades, such as heat pump installation, solar grid maintenance or sustainable agriculture. She hopes universities will offer a partial minor or a course credit for incoming students who have the climate endorsement.
At the same time, Donald Trump has attacked the climate crisis as a “ hoax ”, and new federal scrutiny of renewable energy projects threatens philanthropic support for such initiatives. The treasury department and Republicans in Congress have targeted the tax-exempt status of non-profits that support climate causes, which Seawell said created a noticeable chilling effect among potential donors.
“Funders are worried,” she said.
The Trump administration has also tried to pull funding from and dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research, the climate research center that helped Muñoz with his school gard

articles.title_orig: Sam Green on his documentary 'The Oldest Person in the World'
articles.title_zh: Sam Green on his documentary 'The Oldest Person in the World'
articles.content_orig:
NPR's Ayesha Rascoe speaks with Sam Green about his new documentary, "The Oldest Person in the World."
Everyone, including you, was at one point the youngest person in the world. But only a very select few get to be the opposite.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: He wants to know how you feel about being 117 years.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #2: Feeling good.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Oh, he's feeling good.
RASCOE: Documentary filmmaker Sam Green spent the last decade following each record holder for the oldest person in the world, from Brooklyn to the south of France, from Brazil to Japan. Why?
SAM GREEN: Because I was so puzzled. Every time the oldest person in the world dies, it's in every newspaper and all over the internet. I was curious why. And I got to say, 10 years later, I'm still curious why (laughter).
RASCOE: Sam Green's new movie is called, "The Oldest Person In The World." A warning - this interview contains mentions of suicide. I asked Sam Green, what he wanted to learn from these supercentenarians?
GREEN: You know, I was middle-aged person, sort of asking big questions about the world and life. And I thought, wow, somebody's been around 115 years old. They'll really know. They'll have some answers. And after a while, I started to see, when you're 115, you're probably not thinking about the big questions anymore. Your world shrinks. You're thinking about a nap later or happy memories of when you were younger, flowers. You know, you're not thinking about what's the meaning of life and stuff like that. So I started to realize that that approach, asking these people the big questions, didn't really make sense, which is not to say I didn't learn things because I did. But it wasn't, what's the meaning of life, and them giving the answer really.
RASCOE: What did you learn?
GREEN: (Laughter) Well, a lot of this is just sort of simple common sense stuff. People who live a long, long time and seem to be healthy in spirit are positive people generally. The woman I filmed in Japan, Kane Tanaka, had had a hard life. She said the important thing to living a long life is not to worry.
RASCOE: A lot of these people that you're meeting in this, we see them sleeping a lot, you know? They're not...
RASCOE: ...Really taking in everything around them.
RASCOE: Is it the positive outlook that unites all of them?
GREEN: It's a couple things. One, it's all women.
GREEN: Many of them are women without children. The first woman we filmed with, I said to her niece, why did Miss Susie (ph) live so long, do you think? And her niece said, Miss Susie did not have the two things that will kill you, a husband and kids.
GREEN: Flip side of the coin is none of these people are alone. They all have community and family. You need people around you. You need love and support and community to live a long life. And they all have it.
(SOUNDBITE OF DOCUMENTARY, "THE OLDEST PERSON IN THE WORLD")
GREEN: Does she know she's the oldest person in the world?
GREEN: Have you told her that?
LAVILLA: Really? She said, really? I can't believe that. I don't know that she get the implication of 116, the oldest person in the world.
RASCOE: Did this movie change the way you think about aging and death?
GREEN: Oh, yeah. It changed the way I think about aging. I don't think I would want to be 115. But I do want to live as long as I possibly can. I'm so curious about the world and the future. What's going to happen? But I think I would want to live as long as I can and be independent.
But also with death, I mean, I think it did help me come to terms with death in some ways because the oldest person in the world, when they die, nobody ever says that person was taken before their time. Nobody ever calls it a tragedy. It's always a natural death at the end of a long life. And that's the way it should be.
The last person I interviewed, Maria Branyas, said, you are young. Now is the time to do good works. What I took from it is, you're young and you're alive, and you have time. And take advantage of it and enjoy it.
RASCOE: While you were filming this documentary, it took 10 years to make. And at a point, you're diagnosed with blood cancer. How are you doing at this moment?
GREEN: I'm doing great. Modern medicine - you know, it's a miracle. So I'm doing really good. But it definitely made me think about our short time on this planet. And it definitely sharpened my sense of all that, as I'm sure it does for everybody who has a kind of brush with mortality.
RASCOE: Yeah. You also opened up about your own grief...
RASCOE: ...Over the loss of your brother. He died by suicide before production began, and I'm so sorry for your loss. You are very open about dealing with questions and regrets. And you say you only have one video of him. Did that drive you to capture more of your own family life in this movie and to really try to make sure that you're capturing these moments?
GREEN: Yes, it did. I mean, it was a shocking discovery. Now we all video things all the time on our phones. You know, with my kid, I have thousands of videos. But when I was making the film and I started looking around for videos of my brother, Dave, who died in 2009, I was shocked that I only had one video of him, which was kind of heartbreaking because in a way, these days, you hang on to people through videos. You know, ultimately, in the grand scheme of things, it's a losing battle, but we try. And that's part of life. And that's part of making documentary films, actually, is trying to hold onto things before they go.
RASCOE: The oldest person in the world, as of the end of your documentary and still, is Ethel Caterham of the United Kingdom. How is she doing?
GREEN: Well, it's funny. Ethel Caterham is the first person who rebuffed my inquiries.
GREEN: So I kind of inquired, and somebody who dealt with her said, no, she's fine. She just doesn't want to be bothered. And I thought, OK, I can accept that. I get that. Like, if you're 115, you don't want to be bothered, that's fine.
RASCOE: (Laughter) Yes, that's your right at that moment.
GREEN: But then I got to say, about maybe six months ago or something, there was a video of her getting a visit from King Charles on the internet. And I was like, are you kidding me? King Charles and not me?
RASCOE: Of course she will allow royalty to come into the house (laughter).
GREEN: And it was funny. She said something to him that I think nobody on earth would also be able to say. She said - to King Charles, she said, you were so cute when you were a baby.
GREEN: She can say that. It was great.
RASCOE: Sam Green is the director of "The Oldest Person In The World." Thank you so much for joining us.
GREEN: Thank you. It's a real pleasure speaking with you.
RASCOE: If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

articles.title_orig: Elena Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka, WTA world No. 1 and No. 2, out of China Open - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: Elena Rybakina and Aryna Sabalenka, WTA world No. 1 and No. 2, out of China Open - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Elena Rybakina must be the least demonstrative athlete on the planet. Nobody has so mastered Rudyard Kipling’s advice, emblazoned on the entrance to Wimbledon’s Centre Court, about treating triumph and disaster just the same.
Yet even Rybakina was moved to give a double-fisted victory salute after claiming a three-set victory in a wonderful US Open final. Her reaction prompted Martina Navratilova to tell Sky Sports viewers that “I’ve never seen Elena show so much emotion after winning anything.”
A maiden US Open title for the world No 1 🏆 pic.twitter.com/6WJfvitn7f
This has been quite a fortnight for Rybakina, who came in with a damaged Achilles but still scythed her way to her first US Open title, dominating her chief rival Aryna Sabalenka and living up to her recent promotion to the top of the world rankings.
This match felt like watching one of those Japanese monster movies in which two enormous “kaiju” – comic-book characters of mythical size and ferocity – knock seven bells out of each other while tiny townspeople run around in terror.
With Sabalenka’s serve topping out at 117mph, and Rybakina’s at 121mph, we must have been watching the most devastating pairing the game has ever seen. Not even Venus and Serena Williams, when they were contesting eight major finals during the Noughties, were able to hit the ball as hard as this.
Sabalenka and Rybankina have now played four slam finals, with the spoils evenly shared after this 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 grapple in the Apple – as a boxing promoter might have referred to it.
There is certainly something pugilistic about the way these two go toe-to-toe. The emphasis is on landing the first blow, so the rallies tend not to be particularly long: only four points out of 193 went beyond nine shots. But the precision of the ball-striking was breathtaking. At one point in the first set, Rybakina had hit eight winners to just a single unforced error – the sort of ratio to send coaches starry-eyed.
Sabalanka arrived on court in her showy jewellery – which is worth more than £300,000 for the full set, according to the manufacturers – and an orange Nike dress that put one in mind of the Dutch national football team. “Total tennis” may have been the goal, but sometimes your opponent doesn’t allow you to play. This was the case in the early stages as Rybakina – whose own yellow-and-black outfit evoked the natural warning signs of a wasp or hornet – seemed to flush every ball right out of the centre of her racket.
Sabalenka actually did a sterling job of digging herself out of trouble in her service games, saving four of five break points in the first set. But this still wasn’t enough, given that Rybakina was defending her own serve with the same serenity that characterises everything she does.
The polarities reversed in set two, as Sabalenka began to get her flamethrower of a forehand working. After almost 90 minutes of play, she finally chiselled out some break points – two in game 10, which she couldn’t convert, but then another in game 12 which set up the decider.
The huge contrast in personalities became all too evident in set three. Sabalenka appeared to be at war with herself, emoting and venting almost as if she were an actress projecting her feelings to the whole of this 24,000-seater stadium. As she faced the prospect of slipping a double-break down, she hunkered down on her haunches in despair.
Meanwhile, Rybakina could have been relaxing in a flotation tank for all the stress she showed. Admittedly, she did hit a couple of double-faults as she served out for victory, but she also came up with two aces and two forehand winners in the same game.
Sabalenka, meanwhile, allowed her racket to slip to the ground in frustration and barely managed a brief embrace at the net. While Rybakina was taking the applause of the crowd, Sabalenka was shown smashing her racket.
Sabalenka also appeared to tell a camera operator to “f--- off” as they filmed her following the defeat.
pic.twitter.com/6fJsdiSDir
She had earned a code violation in the first set for slamming a ball out of the stadium, and could easily have picked up a second – and thus a point penalty – after another ball that she batted away struck a cameraman, but chair umpire Greg Allensworth showed leniency.
Asked about tossing her racket, Sabalenka said: “ It’s really tough to control your emotions when you lose in the final of the Grand Slam and when you were trying to go for three-peat. So I just wanted to let it go, because if I would hold it inside, right now or here or there on the court, I wouldn’t be able to say a word or I would just go not really nice over there.
“So I just wanted to let all of that aggression and disappointment go outside.”
The trophy was presented by 2006 champion Maria Sharapova – one of the few women who can look down on 6ft Rybakina, especially when wearing heels. The fans in Arthur Ashe Stadium had given at least 80 per cent of their support to Sabalenka, who won the previous two US Opens on this court, but they applauded warmly, knowing when they had seen a performance for the ages.
Sabalenka wept as she told the fans that “I wish I could have performed a little bit better,” but she did also manage some gracious words of congratulation to her chief rival. Rybakina’s speech was relatively short but to the point, explaining that she had never previously prospered at this event, where her deepest run in seven appearances had stopped at the fourth round.
“The quiet man is turning up the volume,” said the former Tory leader Ian Duncan Smith, in an attempt to position himself as a credible prime minister. Change the sex of that comment, and he could have been talking about Elena Rybakina.
That brings our live coverage of tonight’s final to a close. Make sure to join us for the men’s final tomorrow evening, when American hopeful Ben Shelton meets Alexander Zverev, which gets underway at 7pm.
The new No 1 steps up onto the makeshift stage and begins thanking her team, the sponsors and Sabalenka.
She recovered brilliantly after losing the second set and was the better player in the decider.
She adds the 2026 US Open crown to her Australian Open win in January and her Wimbledon title from 2022 and is presented with a $5.5m cheque. Not bad for a fortnight’s work. Maria Sharapova is on hand to present her with the trophy.
“I want to say thank you of course to all of the spectators for an amazing atmosphere. I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years and it was never successful, nothing close to that and it’s just incredible. I’m falling in love with New York more and more. It’s amazing memories for me.
“Of course, I want to say thank you to the people who without I wouldn’t be here. My team, Stefano [Vukov], Stas [Stanislav Khmarskyi], my fitness coach is back home stressing in front of the TV. Of course, my family also back home and all of my friends. Thank you so much guys, you are the best and without you it wouldn’t be possible.
“Lastly, I want to say thank you to all people who made this tournament possible. It’s an amazing event and I can’t find the words. This atmosphere is just something unbelievable and it doesn’t feel real for now. Thank you so much. I’m looking forward to coming back next year.”
Having sat in her coaches’ box, rather than on her courtside chair, she gives a short speech and appears visibly emotional. She is clearly disappointed to not have achieved the ‘three-peat’.
.. before Sabalenka throws her racket on the court with some force, damaging it in the process. She does, of course, have a history of smashing her racket - she memorably did so in the locker room after losing the 2023 US Open final to Coco Gauff. But to do so on court right after losing a final is somewhat unsavoury.
One more hold of serve and Rybakina can call herself a US Open champion.. what has Sabalenka got left?
Rybakina looks so locked in and she ekes out a 30-0 lead.. only to double fault. She somehow manages to land in a cross-court forehand

articles.title_orig: Chick-fil-A wants to stay a family business even as it expands in the U.S. and abroad
articles.title_zh: Chick-fil-A wants to stay a family business even as it expands in the U.S. and abroad
articles.content_orig:
With restaurants as far-flung as Singapore, Chick-fil-A has expanded far beyond its Southeastern stronghold in recent years, but CEO Andrew Cathy still wants the family-owned business to stay true to its roots.
Nearly five years ago, Cathy succeeded his father, Dan, as chief executive of the chicken chain his grandfather, S. Truett, founded. He took the reins as elevated inflation rocked the restaurant industry and a bevy of new chicken rivals looked to challenge Chick-fil-A's dominance. Since then, not much has changed — except for sluggish traffic across the industry as consumers have become more selective about their dining choices.
The challenging conditions have led to disappointing results for McDonald's , Popeyes, KFC and other restaurant competitors. While Chick-fil-A is not immune to these headaches, Cathy told CNBC that the chain's restaurants have not seen the same downturn.
"This has been a good year," the Atlanta-based Cathy said in downtown Manhattan before a planned activation to raise awareness for the chain's Shared Table hunger relief program.
"Our operators have done such a good job executing on the fundamentals and adding the hospitality to it," he added.
As a privately held business, Chick-fil-A does not report quarterly results. However, franchise disclosures reveal that the company's revenue in 2025 rose 14% to $10.3 billion, while its net income ticked up 1% to $1.05 billion. Its roughly 3,000 locations generated $23.92 billion in system sales last year, making it the third-largest U.S. restaurant by sales, trailing only McDonald's and Starbucks .
Chick-fil-A has no plans for an initial public offering or any other opportunities for outside investment. Cathy said the company plans to stick with its "calculated" and "conservative" growth.
But he may be underselling Chick-fil-A's recent expansion. It opened 179 restaurants last year and has launched in international markets like Canada, Singapore and the United Kingdom in recent years.
Staying private also has advantages, particularly as restaurant stocks have broadly struggled this year. Shares of Jersey Mike's have fallen nearly 28% since its initial public offering in July, while Dunkin' owner Inspire Brands is reportedly unlikely to go public this year unless the sector's performance improves.
"We're able to plan for the quarter century, and we don't have to plan for the quarter," Cathy said.
During Cathy's tenure so far, Chick-fil-A has pursued bold ideas for future growth, like a $1 billion international expansion plan and Daybright, a new beverage-focused restaurant concept created by its venture arm.
But the company is trying to balance those new strategies with its existing traditions.
"I look at driving this business like driving a race car — there's a reason that the windshield's bigger than the rearview mirror," Cathy said. "It's important for the rear view to be grounded on where you are, and there are things that we think about our purpose, our mission, that won't change, but everything else we have to be able to evolve and change."
Some tenets, like staying closed on Sundays, will never change. Others, like its restaurants' signature Southern hospitality, will evolve as diners change their ordering and eating habits.
Cathy said that Chick-fil-A takes a "human plus" approach to technology in its restaurants.
"We think about all these new things into the future, about how will people want to receive food in the future?" he said. "As you think about drone delivery and all the other kind of things that could be coming, it's a fun time in the industry, to think about all the possibilities of what we can do to make a better experience for our guests."
While Chick-fil-A is exploring opportunities to use artificial intelligence behind the scenes, he said that its restaurants will not pursue AI voice ordering in its drive-thru lanes, unlike many of its industry rivals. McDonald's, for example, said at its investor day in September that it plans to test Archy, its voice AI tech, to take orders in both English and Spanish.
"From our experience, we really want that hospitality to be human to human," Cathy said. "We're not gonna substitute that interaction with technology, because we feel like that hospitality is so important to create that warm environment for consumers."
Other restaurants are also refocusing on hospitality, hoping that the extra effort from employees will encourage customers to come back. Starbucks bought around 200,000 Sharpie markers so its baristas could write friendly messages on customers' coffee cups. Burger King has redefined its restaurant manager role into a "Your Way Champion," who greets diners and fixes botched orders. And starting Monday, McDonald's will begin its "Make It Golden" training program for franchisees and employees, which focuses on hospitality as well as food quality.
Chick-fil-A's long-standing focus on service has made it the fast-food leader in customer satisfaction for more than a decade, according to the annual American Customer Satisfaction Index. That reputation can also help the chain stand out from other dining options as consumers have grown more choosy about how they spend their money. Jersey Mike's recently toppled Chick-fil-A in the 2026 study , although Chick-fil-A's score was unchanged from a year ago.
Another enduring element of Chick-fil-A is its famously simple menu. But the chain has even been carefully expanding its offerings, typically through seasonal limited-time items like chicken and waffles or its Honey Pepper Pimento Chicken Sandwich. If a menu item is a "home run," as Cathy calls it, then Chick-fil-A might add it permanently, like its Pineapple Dragonfruit drink line.
"We're very careful about what we want to do, because we want to keep it really focused on unique Chick-fil-A items that they can only get at Chick-fil-A," Cathy said. "But we do want to bring in new flavors and profiles, and that's what we'll do with a lot of our seasonal items that we do, and we learn a lot from our customers about trying those things."
Other fast-food chains are trying to edge into Chick-fil-A's territory. In 2019, Restaurant Brands International's Popeyes sparked the "chicken sandwich wars" by releasing its own version. Chick-fil-A remains the dominant chicken chain in the U.S., with roughly a 43% market share as of 2024, according to Barclays. However, the chicken sandwich helped catapult Popeyes to the No. 2 spot, with about 11% share.
McDonald's could reignite the battle as it prepares to test hand-breaded chicken strips and sandwiches.
But Cathy said that he loves the competition.
"I'm grateful that there's competition in the chicken space, because that means we're in a good space to be," Cathy said. "Competition just makes us better .... What little details can we do to make that environment even more welcoming for customers?"
Chick-fil-A has also innovated outside its restaurants.
In 2017, the company created Red Wagon Ventures, named for the vehicle Truett used to sell bottles of Coca-Cola in his first entrepreneurial gambit at age 6.
"The lion's share of our time and effort is continuing to make sure that we're getting better and better at Chick-fil-A, but we do have a small team that's working and incubating some of these new ideas and thinking about what could be some things that could help us grow into the future," Andrew Cathy said.
Some of those ventures are based in the restaurant industry. Its experimental Little Blue Menu concept served traditional Chick-fil-A menu items along with burgers, pizza and onion rings; the chain will convert its final location into a traditional Chick-fil-A next year. More recently, the subsidiary opened Daybright , which serves coffees, smoothies, juices and doughnuts — but no chicken sandwiches or waffle fries.

Physicists smashed gold nuclei together at nearly the speed of light and found an unexpected pattern in the particles these collisions sprayed out. If confirmed, that pattern could help reveal how the hot soup of quarks and gluons that filled the universe in the first few microseconds after the Big Bang cooled and condensed into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary matter today.
In every collision, particles are flung out sideways; how hard they are flung, on average, varies slightly from one collision to the next. Physicists expected the size of these variations to change smoothly as they adjusted the collision energy. Instead, the variations dipped, shrinking and then growing again. This dip could be a sign of a long-sought "critical point," a special set of conditions at which nuclear matter changes the way it transforms from one form to another.
The signal, detected by the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, is strong enough that it is very unlikely to be a statistical accident. However, the researchers cautioned that the dip is a tantalizing hint, not proof of the long-sought transition. They published their findings Sept. 22 in the journal Physical Review Letters .
Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called quarks, which are held together by the " strong force " carried by particles called gluons. When heated or squeezed enough, protons and neutrons melt into a hot soup of free quarks and gluons known as a quark-gluon plasma. It's thought that this primordial soup of particles filled the universe in the first milliseconds after the Big Bang .
Physicists want to pin down how this soup-ification happened, by measuring the so-called equation of state of nuclear matter. "For water, it tells you how pressure, temperature and density are linked, and therefore when it freezes, boils or expands," study co-author Rutik Manikandhan , a postdoctoral physics scholar at The Ohio State University, told Live Science in an email. For nuclear matter, "it is the basic rulebook for matter under the most extreme conditions in nature, such as the cores of neutron stars," Manikandhan added.
The "critical point" is a key landmark in that rulebook "For water, it is the point where the boundary between liquid and steam disappears," Manikandhan said, and theorists have long suspected that nuclear matter has a similar point. At extremely high temperatures, matter melts smoothly and gradually into quark-gluon plasma, but at higher densities, the change may become abrupt.
The critical point would mark where one kind of transition turns into the other. Some recent calculations place this point within reach of RHIC's lower-energy collisions. "But all of this is still conjectured and there is nothing concrete yet, either from the experimentalists or theorists," Manikandhan said.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The work also matters for cosmology. "Because the matter we create in these collisions resembles the matter that filled the universe a few microseconds after the Big Bang , mapping how it behaves helps us understand how the universe evolved from a hot soup of quarks and gluons into the protons and neutrons that make up everything today," Manikandhan said.
The central part of the three-story STAR detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Scientists recently used the detector to study the conditions of the early universe, just milliseconds after the Big Bang.
To explore this territory, the researchers ran RHIC at a range of collision energies. The lower the energy, the more tightly the colliding matter was squeezed. For its lowest-energy runs, STAR used a "fixed-target" setup, in which a beam of gold nuclei strikes "a thin gold foil placed inside the detector," Manikandhan said, instead of a second, oncoming beam. This produces the densest matter RHIC can make.
Collision energies are measured in electron volts (the energy an electron gains when accelerated across 1 volt). That is a minuscule amount, so particle physicists usually work in billions of electron volts, or giga electron volts (GeV). One GeV is roughly the energy locked up in the mass of a single proton, according to Einstein's famous equation E = mc 2 . The team analyzed roughly 1 billion collisions at energies between 3 and 7.7 GeV per pair of colliding protons or neutrons. That is the bottom of RHIC's range, which reaches 200 GeV.
In each collision, the team measured how hard charged particles were flung sideways out of the fireball ‪—‬ a quantity known as transverse momentum. The researchers then looked for correlations between the particles. A correlation measures whether two things tend to change together. Here, the team checked whether pairs of particles from the same collision tended to both be flung harder than average, or both more gently. That reveals something about the fireball as a whole. If a fireball is slightly hotter, or expands more forcefully, all of its particles get an extra sideways kick together.
"Those correlations reflect how much the temperature and the flow of the fireball fluctuate," Manikandhan said.
Close to a critical point, the matter's heat capacity — the amount of energy needed to raise its temperature — is expected to shoot up. That makes the fireball's temperature harder to budge, so the correlations should weaken. "If the matter approaches a critical point or a phase change, we would expect to see those correlations change in an unusual, non-smooth way as we vary the collision energy," Manikandhan said.
That is what the team saw in the most head-on collisions. "Instead of changing smoothly with energy, the correlations show a dip," Manikandhan said. The researchers compared the data with a smooth trend anchored by earlier STAR measurements at higher energies. The dip departs from that trend with a statistical significance of 5 sigma, the standard physicists usually demand before treating a signal as real. It means that if the true trend were smooth, random scatter in the data would produce such a pronounced dip only about once in 3.5 million tries.
"A smooth trend is what you'd expect from ordinary nuclear matter, so a dip suggests something more interesting is happening at those conditions," Manikandhan said.

articles.title_zh: Israeli investigators believe FlyDubai alleged hijacker was likely lone wolf, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The FlyDubai alleged attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to people familiar with the matter.
The investigation is still in full swing and all avenues are still being explored, the people familiar told CBS News.
The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.
The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot is currently in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing a second round of interrogation after first being questioned by Saudi authorities when the plane made its emergency landing. Israel has sent its own representatives to the UAE to participate in the investigation.
President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Netanyahu told CBS News on Wednesday that the co-pilot's motives are still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, adding, "I think it looks like a suicide attempt."
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.
Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.
At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.
Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.
The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

articles.title_orig: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.title_zh: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.content_orig:
An appeal for wars to end and for peace to be built. The Pope renewed this appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer he led from the window of the Apostolic Palace. As he did during his recent visit to Lourdes, France, he again urged everyone to pray the Rosary for peace and unity in the world, standing in solidarity with children who have already begun doing so through the initiative of the Aid to the Church in Need Foundation, âOne Million Children Praying the Holy Rosary.â
âI wholeheartedly thank all the boys and girls who are joining in this prayer in so many parts of the world.  Let us all follow their example, invoking the intercession of the Virgin Mary so that peoples may be freed from the scourge of war.  In particular, let us pray for the Holy Land and for the innocent victims of violence.â
The campaign began at the start of October with the Pope in the Vatican Gardens and will continue until October 7, the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. This allows dioceses, parishes, schools, communities, and families on different continents to choose the day that is most suitable for dedicating to this particular intention.
Pope Leo then announced that, on the occasion of the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, Pope Francisâs post-synodal apostolic exhortation, a week-long gathering will begin next Wednesday, October 7.
It will be held in his presence in the Paul VI Hall, with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, to take stock of the situation of families today. The gathering will include testimonies from bishops and married couples from the five continents.
It will be an opportunity to listen to the voice of the Church at a time of profound change and to find ways to renew and strengthen the choice of marriage, which in various contexts has experienced dramatic declines over the decades. The Pontiff described it this way:
âIt will be a time of synodal discernment for identifying the steps to be taken in order to proclaim the Gospel today among families and the younger generations.  I entrust this task to your prayers and, above all, the families who, with Godâs help, are a sign of hope and an inestimable treasure for the Church and for society.â
The Pope then once again held up Saint Francis as a model, as he had done during the catechesis, on the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis. He expressed his happiness at the many commemorative initiatives, particularly those held in Assisi with the participation of Italyâs highest state authorities. He also offered a special greeting:
âI also greet the amateur radio operators of Assisi and Foligno who spread Saint Francisâ message of peace.â

articles.title_orig: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.title_zh: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.content_orig:
As Pacific leaders, communities and civil society gather in Fiji and Tuvalu for the Pre-COP31 meetings, the expected absence of many world leaders must not become another excuse for climate inaction, Amnesty International said today.
The meetings come after an unusually hot European summer, with August 2026 becoming the joint-hottest month on record. Against the looming threat of a powerful El Niño, widespread wildfires, droughts, and floods, the new UN warning of the world rapidly breaching warming thresholds adds urgency to the need for decisive climate action.
“World leaders have spent years talking about the climate threats facing the Pacific. Now they must come to Fiji and Tuvalu, listen to Pacific communities and act. Rising seas are already eating away at people’s lands, livelihoods and cultures. Concern without action will not hold back the tide,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Those who do not show up in person cannot evade their responsibilities. Their absence will not stop the seas from rising or erase the obligations of high-emitting countries towards communities paying the highest price for a crisis they did least to cause.
“An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.”
Fiji’s Environment Minister has said that the Pacific-led summit will proceed “with or without” major world leaders .
An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.
Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries . Rising seas, extreme heat, droughts and saltwater intrusion are threatening people’s rights to water, food, health, adequate housing and a safe future. Tuvalu contributes less than 0.003% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it faces some of the climate crisis’ most severe consequences.
During her visit to Tuvalu in 2025, Agnès Callamard witnessed efforts by communities and the authorities to reclaim land from the advancing sea and enable people to remain in their homeland.
“To any world leader who hesitates to confront the biggest crisis of our time, I say this: come to Tuvalu. Speak to people living with rising seas and extreme heat. Witness their daily struggle to adapt, protect their rights and push back against the impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. The reclaimed land in Tuvalu is not a tourist backdrop. It represents a country fighting for its survival,” said Agnès Callamard.
Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts.
“The Pacific should not have to plead for the world’s attention. Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative,” said Agnès Callamard.
“Governments must end fossil fuel use and expansion through just transitions that leave no one behind, tax big polluters and deliver scaled up grants-based climate finance, providing climate reparations and ensuring communities on the front lines of the climate crisis have the resources and power to determine their own futures. The Pacific is sounding the alarm. If the world fails to act here, it will fail everywhere.”
Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative
As President of Negotiations at COP31, Australia has a particular responsibility to stand with its Pacific neighbours and secure an ambitious, human rights-centred outcome. Australia cannot credibly claim climate leadership while continuing to support fossil fuel expansion that deepens the harms facing Pacific communities.
Based on Amnesty International’s recommendations ahead of COP31 , Australia and other governments must use pre-COP31 to advance three priorities:
“Pacific leadership has helped keep the fight for 1.5°C alive, but Pacific communities cannot carry the burden of global climate leadership alone,” said Agnès Callamard. “Australia must use its presiding role to turn Pacific demands into COP31 outcomes, starting with stopping the crisis at source through a just transition away from fossil fuels.”
Governments cannot deliver climate justice while excluding affected communities or silencing those who challenge harmful projects. Across the world, Indigenous Peoples, environmental human rights defenders and communities on the front lines of the climate crisis are resisting fossil fuel expansion and fighting for fairer, more sustainable futures. Yet many face harassment, surveillance, criminalization, violence and restrictions on peaceful protest.
Australia’s treatment of peaceful climate activists will be an important test of its climate leadership. There are also concerns about restrictions on freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly in Fiji.
Ahead of COP31, Amnesty International is launching a global campaign “ Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions ” spotlighting environmental human rights defenders and the alternatives they are fighting for around the world. This includes the First Nations people in Australia , who are challenging offshore oil and gas exploration affecting their lands and waters.
The campaign will show what resistance, dignity and a people-powered just transition can look like when communities refuse to see their lands, waters and futures sacrificed for fossil fuel profits.
Australia and Fiji must ensure that civil society, Indigenous Peoples, affected communities and environmental defenders can participate, speak out and protest peacefully without discrimination, intimidation or reprisals.
“Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions,” said Agnès Callamard.
“COP31 must deliver more than promises. Anything less would betray our shared responsibility to uphold human rights and secure climate justice.”
Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions
The Pacific-led pre-COP31 meetings will take place in Nadi, Fiji, and Tuvalu from 5 to 8 October 2026. COP31 will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.content_orig:
Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates
Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s epicenter.
Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of controversial health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .
Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own.
Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest amount of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin , the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster.
“We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.”
She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”.
She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.”
Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine.
“We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said.
But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease.
“By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.”
She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.”
Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it is a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania will begin to see measles cases.
“We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.”
after newsletter promotion
Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status.
“Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.”
Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency is facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus.
Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year.
“They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.”
For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county.
“We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.”
She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.”
The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment.
